speaker: NORA
text: Imagine you run a power station, and during a planned outage your engineers find damage on the face of a huge flange on a turbine casing. The casing weighs many tonnes. It's bolted into the building. You can't put it on a truck and send it to a machine shop.

speaker: JAMES
text: And the clock is running. The outage window is fixed. Every extra day offline costs money, and the grid operator is expecting you back. So what do you do? You bring the machine shop to the machine. A crew arrives with portable machine tools, bolts them to your equipment, and machines it in place, to tolerances measured in fractions of a millimetre.

speaker: NORA
text: That's today's company. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's In-Place Machining Company, which the private equity firm lists as based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. It does field machining, metrology, which is precision measurement, and wire cutting, on site at industrial plants.

speaker: NORA
text: And last episode we covered Colt Group, which does leak repair and hot tapping. Some of the same world.

speaker: JAMES
text: Some of the same world, and even some of the same competitors. But a different job. Colt mostly keeps live systems running. In-Place Machining mostly works inside planned outages, restoring and fitting heavy equipment that can't be moved.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: deal announcements, trade press, the company's own news pages and some market research headlines. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a figure comes from the company or a data aggregator, we'll flag it. And none of this is investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And a strong caution today. This is one of the thinnest public records we've worked with. We found no dated news about the company in the last two years. Most of what we know is from deal announcements between 2016 and 2023 and from headlines. So we'll be explicit about what's confirmed and what isn't.

speaker: NORA
text: Understood. One sentence, then.

speaker: JAMES
text: In-Place Machining sends skilled crews with portable machine tools and precision measuring equipment to industrial sites, to repair, resurface, cut, align and measure large equipment where it stands, usually during tight maintenance outages.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because through a series of acquisitions it has assembled something unusual: machining and metrology under one roof. Metrology produces detailed digital measurements, including 3D scans of equipment. That's data. And data is exactly where AI could help a field services business quote faster, plan better and do less rework. The question is whether that data is being used.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where is it, and how big is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Levine Leichtman lists the company in Milwaukee. One business listing also shows an address in Huntley, Illinois, under a similar name, which we couldn't reconcile. So: Milwaukee as the private equity firm describes it, with a possible location in northern Illinois.

speaker: NORA
text: And founding date?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find one. An adviser's deal page has a headline describing the sale of a family-held industrial service business, which suggests family roots before private equity arrived, but we only saw the title, so I'll leave it there.

speaker: NORA
text: Size?

speaker: JAMES
text: No employee count or revenue in public sources. There's a figure attributed to the company's website, which we couldn't re-check, of around eighteen thousand customers in more than eighty-five countries. I'd treat that as a company claim, and probably a cumulative count of customers served over many years rather than active accounts. But it does suggest a long history and international reach.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Dean Flint is listed as president and chief executive, according to a business database profile. We didn't find other named leaders.

speaker: NORA
text: And what does it actually do? Break down the three services.

speaker: JAMES
text: Field machining first. That's machining operations done on site with portable equipment. Resurfacing flange faces, boring out holes, milling flat surfaces, cutting and bevelling pipe, turning shafts, all on equipment too large or too fixed to move. Second, metrology. Measuring large equipment precisely, using tools like laser trackers and 3D scanners, so you know exactly what shape it's in, whether it's aligned, and what a replacement part needs to fit. Third, wire cutting, which in general terms means using a diamond wire saw to cut through very large or thick structures, steel or concrete, for demolition, decommissioning or removal.

speaker: NORA
text: Those sound like three different businesses.

speaker: JAMES
text: They're related. Think about a big repair job. You measure the equipment first, to know what's wrong. You cut out the damaged section if needed. You machine the surfaces back to specification. You measure again to prove it's right. A provider that can do all of that is more useful than three separate contractors who have to coordinate inside a tight outage.

speaker: NORA
text: Tell me more about wire cutting. It sounds dramatic.

speaker: JAMES
text: It can be. As general background, diamond wire cutting uses a loop of steel cable studded with industrial diamond segments, pulled at speed through the material by a machine. It can cut through very thick steel or reinforced concrete, in awkward places, without the heat and sparks of torch cutting. That makes it useful where hot work is dangerous, or for cutting large structures into pieces that can be lifted out.

speaker: NORA
text: Where would a customer use that?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, decommissioning old plant, removing large components during a major repair, cutting through heavy foundations, or dismantling structures. We don't have a breakdown of In-Place Machining's wire cutting work, so I won't claim specific markets. But it fits the pattern: heavy, awkward, high-stakes jobs on equipment that can't go anywhere.

speaker: NORA
text: And the company has a page on critical infrastructure.

speaker: JAMES
text: It has a news page titled In-Place Machining for Critical Infrastructure, and there's a feature in IBTimes with a headline about the high-stakes engineering keeping critical infrastructure running. We weren't able to read either, and the IBTimes piece may well be sponsored content. But the positioning is clear: the company wants to be seen as essential to keeping heavy infrastructure working.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the ownership history.

speaker: JAMES
text: In November 2016, Platte River Equity, a private equity firm, invested in In-Place Machining. Under Platte River, in July 2021, the company bought Exact Metrology, which is the first big step into measurement.

speaker: NORA
text: And then the sale.

speaker: JAMES
text: In September 2021, Levine Leichtman, together with management, acquired In-Place Machining from Platte River. The announcement was on the twenty-second of September 2021. The seller was advised by Cleary Gull. The investment was made from Levine Leichtman's lower middle market fund.

speaker: NORA
text: So the current owner has held it for about five years.

speaker: JAMES
text: A little over five years. In private equity terms, that's a mature hold. Which means the question of what the company looks like to a future buyer is becoming more relevant.

speaker: NORA
text: Do we know what the 2021 buyer was supposed to bring?

speaker: JAMES
text: Only indirectly. The adviser's deal page headline talks about selling to a financial buyer that can build corporate infrastructure to take advantage of significant growth opportunities. We only saw the headline, but the phrase is telling. Corporate infrastructure means things like finance systems, HR, safety programmes, sales and, in our view, shared technology and data. The things a founder-scale business often lacks and a platform needs before it can absorb acquisitions smoothly.

speaker: NORA
text: So the plan was to build the platform and then buy onto it.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's how we read it. And the acquisitions that followed fit that plan. Whether the infrastructure kept up with the deals is the open question.

speaker: NORA
text: What has it bought under the current owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: Quite a lot, at least through early 2023. In October 2021, just a month after the deal, OASIS Alignment Services, which was reported in the paper industry trade press, so it likely brought expertise in aligning the large rolls used in paper mills. In December 2022, East Coast Metrology, a second measurement business. In March 2023, Western Machine Works, announced as a Levine Leichtman portfolio company deal. And there are two more on the company's own news pages, Baton Rouge Machine Works, also called BR Machine, and WL3 Solutions, which we couldn't date.

speaker: NORA
text: So six acquisitions in total, if you include Exact Metrology before the current owner.

speaker: JAMES
text: At least six across sources. One data aggregator headline counts four acquisitions, which doesn't match, so the exact count is uncertain. But the pattern is clear. Machining capacity, metrology capability, alignment expertise, and regional bases, including, judging by the name, Baton Rouge on the Gulf Coast.

speaker: NORA
text: And since March 2023?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the puzzle. We found nothing dated since then. No acquisitions, no leadership changes, no product announcements, no layoffs, no lawsuits. It's possible the company has simply been quiet while integrating. It's possible there's news we couldn't reach. But publicly, the trail goes cold in early 2023.

speaker: NORA
text: How should listeners read that?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cautiously. Silence isn't evidence of trouble. Many industrial services companies don't issue press releases unless they're buying something. But after a run of five deals in eighteen months, a long quiet period is consistent with a company digesting what it bought. That's our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer problem. Why does a plant need machining done on site?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because some equipment simply can't go to a shop. A turbine casing, a large pump housing, a heat exchanger, a paper machine roll, a ship's stern tube, a hydroelectric generator component. They're too big, too heavy, or built into the structure. Taking them out means cutting through walls or dismantling half the plant, which would take far longer than the repair itself.

speaker: NORA
text: So the alternative to field machining is what?

speaker: JAMES
text: Often, a much longer outage, or replacing equipment that could have been repaired. As general background, plants plan major maintenance outages, sometimes called turnarounds in refining or outages in power, and they pack a huge amount of work into a fixed window. When inspection during the outage reveals damage, the repair has to fit inside that window. Field machining makes that possible.

speaker: NORA
text: Who's the buyer?

speaker: JAMES
text: Mostly maintenance teams at plants, and the maintenance and service teams at equipment manufacturers, the companies that make turbines, pumps or paper machines and service them for their customers. Procurement is typically led by maintenance, with a lot of repeat customers. That's our inference from how the service works.

speaker: NORA
text: What do they care about?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, three things in this order. First, time to return to service. Can you finish inside the window? Second, getting it right. The work has to be in specification first time, because rework inside an outage is a disaster. Third, the credentials and experience of the crew. Price matters, but when an outage day can cost far more than the machining job itself, a cheap contractor who overruns is very expensive.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is rework such a disaster?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because inside an outage, everything is sequenced. The machining has to finish before the reassembly crew can start, before the inspection, before the restart. If a surface is machined out of specification and has to be redone, every trade waiting downstream waits too. One day's rework can push the whole outage back a day. That's why buyers value providers who measure carefully before and after, and why metrology and machining belong together.

speaker: NORA
text: And the equipment manufacturers? You said they're customers too.

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, yes. A turbine or pump manufacturer often services its installed base, and when a repair needs in-place machining, it may subcontract to a specialist rather than keep its own field machining crews everywhere. For a provider, being the trusted subcontractor to a manufacturer's service team can be a steady source of work. We don't know which manufacturers, if any, In-Place Machining works with, so that's general industry background.

speaker: NORA
text: And the measurement side?

speaker: JAMES
text: Metrology is increasingly the front end of these jobs. Before you machine anything, you need to know exactly what you're dealing with. How much material has to come off? Is the surface warped? Will the replacement part fit? A 3D scan gives you a precise digital model of the equipment as it actually is. That's valuable on its own, and it's also the starting point for designing and machining replacement parts.

speaker: NORA
text: What's driving demand?

speaker: JAMES
text: Our inference is three things. Ageing plant assets that can't be moved to a shop and are often cheaper to repair than replace. Pressure to keep outage windows short. And growing use of 3D scanning and measurement data to fit replacement parts accurately.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go inside a job. What does field machining actually look like?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, a crew arrives with portable machine tools. Some clamp onto a flange and rotate around it to resurface the face. Some bore out holes in place. Some are portable milling machines that run along a rail bolted to the equipment. Some cut and bevel pipe. The technician sets the tool up precisely on the equipment, which is the hard part, then makes careful cuts, measuring as they go.

speaker: NORA
text: And the setup is the skill.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. On a shop floor, you have a rigid machine bolted to the floor and the workpiece clamped to it. In the field, the workpiece is the machine's foundation. You might be working sideways, upside down, in a cramped space, in heat. Getting the tool aligned and rigid enough to cut to tight tolerances is a craft. That's why experienced field machinists are so valuable and so hard to replace.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the life of a field crew like?

speaker: JAMES
text: Demanding, in general. Crews travel to wherever the equipment is, often at short notice, and outage work tends to run long shifts, sometimes around the clock, to finish inside the window. Sites have their own safety rules, inductions and permits. Work can be in confined spaces, at height or in heat. Safety is paramount, and so is planning, because a crew that arrives with the wrong tool or a missing fixture loses hours it can't get back.

speaker: NORA
text: So logistics is part of the skill.

speaker: JAMES
text: A big part. The right equipment, the right fixtures and the right people, at the right site, on the right day. In a company with several regional bases, getting that right across the network is a real operational capability, and it's a place where better data and planning tools can help.

speaker: NORA
text: And metrology on site?

speaker: JAMES
text: Typically a laser tracker or a 3D scanner. A laser tracker measures specific points very accurately over large distances, so you can check alignment of, say, a line of bearings or the flatness of a large surface. A 3D scanner captures millions of points to build a digital model of a surface or a whole component. Both produce data files that engineers analyse, often in computer-aided design software.

speaker: NORA
text: And alignment, from OASIS?

speaker: JAMES
text: In a paper mill, for example, there are many large rolls that the paper web runs over at speed. If they're not aligned precisely, you get problems with quality and wear. Alignment services measure and correct that. OASIS's deal being reported in the paper trade press suggests that's where its expertise lay, and Western Machine Works also appears to have a paper roll repair background, judging by how its deal was framed.

speaker: NORA
text: What happens to the data after a job?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the big question. In many field services businesses, scan files sit on an engineer's laptop or a project folder, job notes sit in a report, and setups and lessons learned sit in the technician's memory. We have no evidence of how In-Place Machining handles this. But it's where the AI opportunity starts.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do a walk-through. A hypothetical job, invented customer, invented people.

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's say a paper mill in the Pacific Northwest has a ten-day planned outage. During inspection, the maintenance manager, call her Linda, finds that the bearing housing on a large dryer roll is worn and the roll alignment along that section of the machine is off. She calls a field machining provider, a company like In-Place Machining.

speaker: NORA
text: What happens today?

speaker: JAMES
text: An estimator takes the call and asks for photos, drawings, dimensions, access details and the outage dates. Often there's a site visit to scope the job. The estimator then works out the crew, the equipment and the time required, partly from experience and partly from records of similar jobs, if they can find them. A quote goes back to Linda, maybe after a day or two. Meanwhile her outage clock is ticking.

speaker: NORA
text: Then the crew arrives.

speaker: JAMES
text: A metrology technician scans the bearing housing and measures the roll alignment. The data goes to an engineer, who works out how much material to remove and what the finished dimensions need to be. The field machinists set up a portable boring bar, machine the housing back to specification, and the metrology tech measures again. The alignment crew adjusts the roll positions. A report goes to Linda with before and after measurements.

speaker: NORA
text: And it fits in the window.

speaker: JAMES
text: Hopefully. But there are risks. If the scope was underestimated, the crew needs more time or more equipment. If the scan reveals something unexpected, the engineering takes longer. If the right specialist is on another job across the country, there's a wait.

speaker: NORA
text: Replay it with AI.

speaker: JAMES
text: Linda sends photos and basic dimensions through a request portal, or even just by email. An assistant structures the request and searches the company's history. Similar jobs, same type of equipment, similar dimensions, maybe even the same mill if they've worked there before. It pulls up the crew sizes, equipment, durations and any surprises on those jobs, and drafts a scope and a quote for the estimator to review. The estimator adjusts and sends it the same day.

speaker: NORA
text: So the estimator starts from evidence.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Then on site, the scan data flows straight into a standard workflow. Software compares the scan to the design dimensions and flags where the material needs to come off, and the engineer reviews it in an hour rather than half a day. Meanwhile the scheduling system has already checked which qualified machinists and which boring equipment are available for those dates.

speaker: NORA
text: And afterwards?

speaker: JAMES
text: The job record, the scans, the setup notes, the duration and any problems all go into a searchable history. So the next estimator quoting a similar job has better data. And Linda gets a digital record of her equipment's condition, which she can use when planning the next outage.

speaker: NORA
text: Does the machinist's job change?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not much on the tool itself. The cutting is still skilled hands-on work. What changes is that the machinist arrives with better information, and their setup notes become a resource for others rather than staying in their head. In my view, AI in this business is about everything around the cutting, not the cutting itself.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do one more, from the inside. A day in the life of an estimator.

speaker: JAMES
text: Invented again. Call him Tom, an estimator at a regional base. Monday morning, he has nine open requests. Two are from regular customers with outages in three weeks. One is an emergency: a refinery found a damaged heat exchanger flange and needs a crew by Wednesday. The rest are budget enquiries for outages next spring.

speaker: NORA
text: Where does he start?

speaker: JAMES
text: With the emergency, obviously. He calls the customer, gets dimensions and photos, and tries to remember a similar job. He thinks one was done at another base two years ago, so he emails a colleague there. The colleague is on site and replies in the evening. Meanwhile Tom builds the quote from his own experience, checks which machinists and which flange facing machines are free, and sends it. He's not sure whether he priced in enough time for setup on that type of exchanger.

speaker: NORA
text: And the budget enquiries wait.

speaker: JAMES
text: They wait. And budget quotes for next year's outages are often where the bigger, more profitable work is won. So the urgent crowds out the important. That's not Tom's fault. It's the shape of the job when knowledge is scattered across bases and people.

speaker: NORA
text: With AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: Tom puts the emergency request into the system and instantly sees the job at the other base, with its scope, setup time, crew, duration and final cost, plus three other similar jobs. He quotes with more confidence in half the time. The system suggests a draft for each budget enquiry based on similar outage work, which he reviews and adjusts. By lunchtime, everything has gone out. The customers get faster answers, and the company wins more of the work it actually wants.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's widen out. How big is this market?

speaker: JAMES
text: There's no reliable figure. One data aggregator report headline puts on-site machining at about three hundred and eighty-nine million dollars by 2033. We didn't check the base year or methodology, and other reports on the same category exist with figures we didn't compare. So treat it as a sign that this is a niche market in the hundreds of millions, not a vast one. That's also a reason consolidation makes sense. A niche, fragmented market is where a platform can become a leader.

speaker: NORA
text: What segments does it serve?

speaker: JAMES
text: Oil and gas, pulp and paper, through the OASIS and Western Machine Works deals, power and critical infrastructure, and general heavy industry. Each has its own outage rhythm and equipment types.

speaker: NORA
text: Take me through them briefly.

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, power generation has turbines, generators, pumps and large valves, with outages planned well ahead and tight return-to-service deadlines. Oil and gas, especially refining, has turnarounds with huge amounts of work packed in, and lots of flanges, heat exchangers and pressure vessels. Pulp and paper has very large rolls and machines running continuously, where alignment and roll repair are critical, which is why the OASIS and Western deals make sense. And critical infrastructure, in general, could include things like hydroelectric plants, water systems or other heavy public assets, though we couldn't read the company's page on it to see exactly what it means.

speaker: NORA
text: So different customers, but the same basic need.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Equipment too big to move, a tight window, and a need for precision. That common need is what lets one platform serve several industries, and it's also why a shared job history across segments is valuable. A setup trick learned on a paper machine might help on a power plant pump.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: At the large end, Hydratight, which is a brand of Enerpac Tool Group after Enerpac acquired it, offers on-site machining alongside its broad flange and bolting business. Team Incorporated, the large inspection and repair group, offers field machining through its Repair360 business, often as part of a bundled turnaround service. Those two were also names we mentioned with Colt.

speaker: NORA
text: And smaller players?

speaker: JAMES
text: A long tail of regional providers. Names we came across include Sealtec USA, LTJ Industrial, Prime Field Service, which describes itself as a millwright and in-place machining contractor, and T and W Valve and Machine Company, a regional machine shop that offers on-site work. And as general industry knowledge, there are companies like Climax that make portable machine tools and also offer services. We didn't verify ownership for most of these.

speaker: NORA
text: So where does In-Place Machining fit?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, as a specialist that bundles machining, metrology, alignment and wire cutting, with regional bases in the Midwest, the Gulf Coast and, it seems, the Pacific Northwest. The big groups can offer broader turnaround packages. The small regionals can be cheap and local. In-Place Machining's pitch is breadth of specialist capability, and the metrology data that most field competitors don't hold.

speaker: NORA
text: And any AI-native challengers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not in field machining itself. But there's a company called CloudNC, which uses AI to generate machining programs, the instructions that tell a computer-controlled machine how to cut, for shop-floor work. Dassault Systemes has written about AI in machining operations too. That's not a competitor for field work, but it shows the direction. AI is shortening programming and planning time in machining generally, which raises the bar for everyone.

speaker: NORA
text: What are the big trends?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four, in my view. Consolidation of metrology, alignment and machining into bundled services, which In-Place Machining's deals follow. Scanning and digital measurement becoming the front end of field jobs. Ageing assets pushing demand toward repair over replacement. And a skilled labour shortage in machining and field trades, which pushes providers toward capturing knowledge and documenting jobs digitally.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's think about the acquisitions as a strategy. What was the logic?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd read it in three layers. First, capability: metrology through Exact and East Coast Metrology, alignment through OASIS, wire cutting through WL3, judging by what the company now offers. Second, geography: Baton Rouge for the Gulf Coast, and Western Machine Works, which we believe gives a base in the West, possibly the Pacific Northwest, though we didn't confirm its location. Third, industry: pulp and paper expertise through OASIS and Western.

speaker: NORA
text: So a one-stop shop for outage work.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the vision, as we read it. A plant can call one provider to measure, cut, machine and align, anywhere in the country.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the integration challenge?

speaker: JAMES
text: Multiple small businesses, different brands, different locations, different systems for quoting, scheduling and reporting. Different scan software and file formats. Different ways of pricing. Each one probably had a strong founder or leader with their own way of doing things. Bringing that together into one platform, with one customer experience, is the hard, unglamorous work of a buy-and-build. We'd guess there's some integration debt across systems, though that's an inference.

speaker: NORA
text: And the cross-sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's where the payoff should come. If a paper mill uses the alignment team, does it also use the machining team? If a refinery uses machining, does it know about metrology or wire cutting? A single customer view across all the businesses would show those gaps. Without it, the group can end up as several companies sharing a logo.

speaker: NORA
text: Is five years enough to have done that integration?

speaker: JAMES
text: It could be, but we have no public evidence either way. That's one of the questions I'd most want answered if I were looking at this business. In my view, the value at exit depends heavily on whether it's one integrated platform or a collection of acquired shops.

speaker: NORA
text: So, the AI question. Where is the company today?

text: We found no evidence of AI. Searches for In-Place Machining and AI turned up only general articles about AI in machining, and CloudNC. No product, partnership, hire or statement. No AI roles.

text: This is the interesting part. Through Exact Metrology and East Coast Metrology, the company holds metrology and scan capability, and presumably years of scan data from customer jobs. But we found no description of a data platform or any claim about using that data. So it's a potential asset whose current state we can't see.

speaker: JAMES
text: The critical infrastructure positioning might imply working under regulated-sector requirements, for example at power stations, but we couldn't read the page to verify. We found no AI governance or information security certification.

text: So, overall?
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: Early. Like most field services companies, and like Colt last episode, In-Place Machining doesn't present itself as a technology company. But it has more digital raw material than most, because of the metrology business. In my view, that's the starting point for its AI story.
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: Why is scan data so useful for AI specifically?
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: Because it's precise, structured and comparable. A 3D scan of a flange or a bearing housing is a set of measured points, not a technician's description. If you have hundreds of scans of similar equipment, along with what was done and how long it took, you can start to learn patterns. How much material typically has to come off a worn surface of this type. How long the machining took for a given amount of wear. Which scans predicted problems that showed up later. Text notes are useful, but measurement data is where a field services company can build something genuinely hard to copy.
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: As long as it's kept, labelled and linked.
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the condition. An unlabelled scan file on an old laptop is just a file. A scan linked to the customer, the equipment, the job, the outcome and the cost is an asset.
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: What would you want to know first?
chapter: Where In-Place Machining is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: Where the scan data lives, in what formats, and how much of it is linked to job records. How estimating is done today across the group, and whether there's a common job history. And how scheduling works across the regional bases. Those answers tell you which AI bet is realistic.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's name the challenges. What's hard, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, the labour model. Every job needs skilled crews on site, travelling to wherever the equipment is. You can't scale that like software. Growth means hiring and developing more field machinists and metrology technicians, who are in short supply.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration debt, which we've discussed. Several acquisitions with different systems, brands and practices.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cyclicality. Demand is tied to heavy-industry capital spending and outage cycles. A downturn in oil and gas, or in power maintenance spending, or a weak paper market, hits volume. Diversification across segments helps, but it doesn't remove the risk.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Competition from bundlers. Team and Enerpac through Hydratight can offer machining as part of broader turnaround packages, which can pressure price. When a refinery hands one big contractor its entire outage scope, the specialist may become a subcontractor, or be left out.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Visibility and momentum. After a run of acquisitions to early 2023, there's no public news. That makes it hard for outsiders to judge momentum, and in my view it's also a missed opportunity. Recruiting skilled people, winning new customers and eventually telling the story to a buyer all benefit from a visible, confident company.

speaker: NORA
text: And the AI-specific challenge?

speaker: JAMES
text: Turning scattered data into something useful. Scan files, job reports, quotes and schedules from multiple acquired businesses, in different formats, possibly on individual laptops. The AI work starts with gathering and structuring that, which isn't exciting but is essential. And then convincing experienced estimators and machinists that the tools help them rather than second-guess them.

speaker: NORA
text: And the people pipeline? You mentioned a labour shortage.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's probably the biggest long-term constraint. Field machining combines machinist skills with the ability to work in difficult field conditions and solve problems on the spot. That takes years to develop. As experienced people retire, their knowledge goes with them unless it's captured. In my view, a company that can train new field machinists faster, through mentoring backed by a good knowledge base, has a real advantage in recruiting and in capacity.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk opportunities. Where would you push first?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first is quote and job-scope automation, using scan data and past job records to draft quotes and scope jobs faster. We walked through it with Linda. The value lever is estimator and engineer hours, and then win rate. In outage work, the provider who sends a credible, well-scoped quote first often wins the job.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: A scan-to-part workflow. Link the metrology data to the computer-aided machining preparation, so a scan flows directly into the plan for what to machine or what replacement part to make. That cuts engineering rework and reduces the risk of a part that doesn't fit. The lever is margin per job.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: A technician knowledge base. Capture field crew know-how on setups, tolerances and tricky equipment, so new hires get productive faster. Imagine a machinist about to set up on an unfamiliar turbine casing being able to pull up how a senior colleague did it two years ago, with photos and notes. The lever is time to productivity, which in a labour shortage is worth a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cross-selling across the stack. Bundle metrology, alignment, machining and wire cutting into outage packages for existing customers. A plant that already trusts the alignment team is a warm lead for machining. The lever is revenue per customer.

speaker: NORA
text: And beyond those?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pricing discipline. Use job history to price by outage window and urgency rather than standard rates. A job that has to be done in a three-day window over a holiday is worth more than one with flexible timing. Geographic expansion, using the Baton Rouge and Western bases to pursue Gulf Coast and Pacific Northwest accounts. And more tuck-in acquisitions in metrology and alignment, which would also build a bigger data asset.

speaker: NORA
text: Customers won't love paying more for urgency.

speaker: JAMES
text: Maybe not, but they understand it, because they know what a lost outage day costs them. In my view, the key is transparency. A clear rate structure for planned work booked early, and a premium for short-notice or compressed-window work, with the reasons explained. It also nudges customers to book earlier, which helps the company plan crews and equipment. Job history tells you which jobs actually cost more to deliver, so the premiums can be grounded in fact rather than guesswork.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a data product here? Selling the scans themselves?

speaker: JAMES
text: Possibly, in my view. A digital record of a customer's critical equipment, scanned at every outage, would let the plant track wear over time and plan replacements. That could become a recurring service: we scan your critical assets every outage and give you a condition report and a forecast. It's speculative, but it's the kind of move that turns a project business into a relationship business.

speaker: NORA
text: And scheduling?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Outage season can be crowded, with many plants scheduling work at similar times of year. Matching qualified crews and specialised equipment to overlapping jobs across regions is a hard optimisation problem, and good scheduling tools could raise utilisation and reduce travel. I'd put it third or fourth, after quoting and the knowledge base.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months, what is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Quote and job-scope automation from scan data and job history. The company already holds scan data from its metrology businesses and runs many similar jobs, which gives it a base to learn from. It saves skilled time, it speeds response, it improves win rate, and the estimator stays in charge of the final number.

speaker: NORA
text: Give me the first hundred days.

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: pick one segment and one region, say power generation jobs out of the main Midwest base. Gather the last few years of quotes, final job costs, durations and scan files for that segment into one place. That alone is probably a project. Sit down with the estimators: how do they quote today, what do they look at, where do they get it wrong. And agree the measures: time to quote, quote accuracy against actual job cost, and win rate.

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?

speaker: JAMES
text: Build a simple tool that, for a new request, finds the most similar past jobs and shows the estimator their scope, crew, equipment, duration and final cost, with a suggested range. Nothing fancy. Run it alongside the normal process. The estimator quotes as usual, then looks at the tool's suggestion, and you record both.

speaker: NORA
text: So shadow mode, again.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the right pattern whenever expert judgement is involved. Days sixty to a hundred: compare the estimator's quotes and the tool's suggestions against how jobs actually turned out. Where the tool was closer, show the team. Where it was wrong, find out why. If it's helping, roll it to the next segment and the acquired businesses, and make recording final job data a standard step at job close.

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The most respected estimator or operations leader, paired with someone who can handle the data. The estimators need to feel this is their tool. If it's seen as head office checking their work, it'll fail.

speaker: NORA
text: Any governance points?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three. Customer scan data belongs to, or is at least shared with, the customer, so agree how it can be used, especially for critical infrastructure clients who may have strict rules. Keep the estimator accountable for every quote. And make sure the data on which the tool learns is clean and consistent, or it'll learn the wrong lessons.

speaker: NORA
text: And the second-best bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: The technician knowledge base. It addresses the labour shortage directly and protects the company against retirements. And it's relatively low risk, because it's guidance for skilled people, not automation of their work.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from In-Place Machining?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, acquisitions buy data, not just revenue. When In-Place Machining bought metrology businesses, it bought scan capability and, presumably, a history of scans. Many companies don't realise what data they acquired, or let it sit in the acquired firm's folders. Inventory it.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, quoting is a great first AI target in project businesses. Every project business quotes. Quotes are slow, they depend on a few experienced people, and accuracy matters a lot for margin. If you have records of past jobs and their final costs, you can help your estimators start from evidence.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, integration has to be finished to pay off. A buy-and-build creates a lot of value on paper. The value only becomes real when customers experience one company, the data flows across the businesses, and cross-selling actually happens. If you can't show that, a buyer will value you as a collection of shops.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, quiet isn't always golden. In a mature hold, telling your story publicly, new capabilities, new customers, how you use technology, helps with recruitment, with customers and with the eventual sale. A company with no public news for over three years makes outsiders guess, and guesses are rarely generous.

speaker: NORA
text: I'd add one: the craft stays human.

speaker: JAMES
text: Agreed. In businesses built on hands-on skill, AI's job is to take the friction out of everything around the craft, quoting, planning, paperwork, knowledge sharing, so the craftspeople can spend more time doing what only they can do.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI-native machining tools lowering barriers. AI-assisted programming and planning tools could help competing shops offer faster, more sophisticated work, though not the field work itself. Two, bundling by large industrial services groups pressuring price. Three, cyclicality in heavy-industry capital spending and outage budgets.

speaker: NORA
text: Four?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four, remote inspection and digital twins. A digital twin is a detailed digital model of a physical asset that's kept up to date with data. As drones, fixed sensors and remote scanning improve, some measurement work that requires a technician on site today might be done remotely. That's our inference, and it cuts both ways: it's a threat to some on-site metrology hours, and an opportunity if In-Place Machining builds those twins itself from its scan history.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: After five years, the question of exit becomes more pressing. The story a buyer will want to hear is an integrated platform with clear cross-selling, good margins and a credible technology plan. AI quoting and a scan data asset would strengthen that story. A collection of loosely connected businesses with no recent news would weaken it.

speaker: NORA
text: Are there AI-specific risks inside the business?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two. First, a quoting tool that learns from bad data. If past job records are incomplete, for example if overruns weren't recorded properly, the tool will systematically underestimate, and the company will win work it loses money on. Second, over-reliance. If estimators stop thinking critically because the tool usually gets close, the unusual job, the one that's different from anything in the history, gets mispriced. The defence is good data at job close, and a culture where the estimator owns the number.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. First, any new public news at all: an acquisition, a leadership announcement, a new capability. That would end the long quiet period. Second, any sign of a digital platform, a customer portal for scan data or condition reports, or a technology leadership hire. Third, any sign of a sale process, given the length of the hold.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does In-Place Machining sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: Precision machining, measurement and cutting, done where the equipment stands.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Skilled field crews, plus a metrology business that generates real data.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: A thin public record and probable integration debt from many acquisitions.

speaker: NORA
text: Shipped AI feature?

speaker: JAMES
text: None we found.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Quoting and job scoping from scan data and job history.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace the field machinist?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. You can't upload a turbine casing. It will make the machinist's preparation and paperwork much easier.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a plant maintenance manager should ask their machining provider this year?

speaker: JAMES
text: Can you give me the scan data from my last outage, and compare it at the next one?

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cautiously optimistic. The capabilities are real and the data is promising. I'd want evidence that the integration is done.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. In-Place Machining Company, which Levine Leichtman lists in Milwaukee, does field machining, metrology and wire cutting on heavy equipment that can't be moved, usually inside tight outage windows. Platte River Equity invested in 2016 and bought Exact Metrology in 2021. Levine Leichtman and management acquired it in September 2021, followed by OASIS Alignment Services, East Coast Metrology, Western Machine Works, and later Baton Rouge Machine Works and WL3 Solutions, building a one-stop outage provider across paper, power, oil and gas and heavy industry. Chief executive Dean Flint leads it. We found no public news since March 2023 and no evidence of AI. The best opportunity, in our view, is AI-assisted quoting and job scoping from scan data and job history, followed by a technician knowledge base. The challenges are the skilled labour model, integration, cyclicality and competition from big bundled providers.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the lesson is that in a business built on hands-on skill, the data you collect around the work, every scan, every quote, every setup note, can become as valuable as the work itself, if you gather it in one place.

speaker: NORA
text: Next time on Portfolio Deep Dives, episode twenty-one, we head back to Houston for USA Industries, the maker of tube plugs and pipe-isolation tools, which joined the portfolio less than a year ago.

speaker: JAMES
text: See you then.
